Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is 9to5Mac's weekly series highlighting the latest apps from the indie app community. If you're a developer and want to get your app featured, please reach out to us.

iOS 27 was released to the public about two weeks ago, and its flagship feature is undoubtedly Siri AI. While Siri AI represents a revolutionary leap compared to previous versions, it still has its shortcomings. QuillCue aims to fill one of those gaps by offering a custom keyboard that lets you save prompts for later use.

Key features

QuillCue is a really impressive concept. Through iOS's custom keyboard feature, it lets you insert pre-written prompts into Siri AI. Simply swipe down from the top of the screen, switch to the custom keyboard, select your prompt, and hit enter.

If you have questions you regularly ask Siri but don't want to type out the same thing every time, this can save you a ton of time. One of the default prompts is searching for nearby coffee shops that allow remote laptop work. Since results are location-dependent, you always get fresh information and might discover places you never knew existed — really handy.

Of course, you can pre-write any prompt that Siri AI is capable of handling. QuillCue saves you from having to dictate or re-type it each time, making Siri AI much more convenient to use.

If you need to craft a lengthy, multi-step prompt, QuillCue can save you a huge amount of time — because Siri AI currently lacks the concept of 'skills' and doesn't learn from your habits. The use cases are virtually endless. The app also offers folders, making it easy to organise and categorise your different prompts.

Finally, it also supports importing and exporting your prompt library, so you can share prompts with friends or move them between devices.

Download the app

QuillCue is available for free on the App Store, with no ads or in-app purchases. For the latest updates, you can follow developer Parker Ortolani on X.

This app requires an iPhone running iOS 27.0 or later and is currently limited to users in the United States.
